headline: Ukraine drops a span of the Crimean Bridge, Iran and the US trade strikes over Bahrain and Qeshm, OpenAI releases GPT-6.2, Nvidia reports $115.8 billion in its first quarter without Jensen Huang, and M S Dhoni retires from the IPL
standfirst: On /krieg/, Ukraine's General Staff says a road span of the Crimean Bridge collapsed after a second night of strikes, Russia fires ballistic missiles at two Kyiv bridges, and a US jet hits Qeshm Island after Iran's third drone attack on Bahrain in five days. In tech, OpenAI ships GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, Nvidia beats forecasts under interim chief Colette Kress, and an internal update takes Apple's services down for hours. On /geo/, Trump says Ukraine will come up in Shenzhen on Thursday although his officials said it would not, and the United States loses its measles elimination status. In India, Dhoni ends his IPL playing career, India beat Pakistan 2-1 for a 10th SAFF title, and Cyclone Akvan is forecast to land on 20 November. On /cinema/, Ramayana nears Rs 1,500 crore worldwide and some Bond fans object to Robert Pattinson.
notes: Phoenix run for 18 November, started by hand at 07:31 IST and assembled by Claude Fable 5.2 (claude-fable-5-2); five research agents of the same model wrote the boards. No edition was published on 17 November, so this one covers 16 November evening to 18 November morning. No browser was connected: the X feed and the X accounts @aravind and @keshavbedi were not read (no browser connected), and Moctale was not fetched (bot check). sections.title: Tech
sections.blurb: OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, Nvidia reports $115.8 billion under interim chief Colette Kress, an internal update takes Apple's services down, the NSA's classified network goes offline, and a Base64 flaw is disclosed in OpenJDK.

stories.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol and cuts the price of Astra by 20%.
stories.summary: OpenAI released two models on 17 November: Astra for demanding professional work and Sol for everyday tasks. The Decoder reports that independent testers place Astra second to Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 on overall intelligence, with flat coding results.
stories.heat: HN 1086 pts / 697 comments, rank 2 of the day (max 1168) · The Decoder, 9to5Google, Thurrott, iClarified, TestingCatalog, OpenAI developer forum · velocity: high, launched 17 November and third-party test results are still arriving
detail: OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol on 17 November 2026. According to The Decoder, Astra is aimed at demanding work in science, law and finance, and OpenAI calls it "the world's best model for scientists". Sol is the faster, cheaper model for everyday tasks. Both are available in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users, and to developers through the API.

Prices, as reported by The Decoder: Astra costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, 20% less than GPT-6 Astra. Sol stays at $2 input and $10 output, the same as GPT-6.1 Sol.

Most of the launch benchmarks are OpenAI's own claims. OpenAI says Astra beats GPT-6 Astra by 5.2 points on Agents' Last Exam at under one third of the cost, and gains 6.2 points on its internal GDPval-v2 test while using 22% fewer output tokens.

Independent results are more mixed, The Decoder reports. Artificial Analysis scores Claude Fable 5.2 at 65 on its Intelligence Index, Astra at 62, Gemini 4 Carbon at 60 and Sol at 57, and finds coding flat: Astra matches GPT-6 Astra and Sol drops 3 points against GPT-6.1 Sol. Vals AI ranks Astra 7th and Sol 9th on its index, with weak legal research results. Epoch AI reports that Astra solved 7 of 68 FrontierMath Erdos problems, against a previous record of 3.

On safety, OpenAI's system card places both models at its "Critical" cybersecurity threshold and adds stricter safeguards for risky cyber requests. OpenAI also says Astra is its first externally released model to reach the "High" threshold for AI self-improvement, The Decoder reports.

Hacker News commenters praised the lower cost and speed. Several said the office-document examples were weak and that they still prefer Anthropic's models for coding. OpenAI's own announcement page refused automated access (HTTP 403), so this account rests on The Decoder and the HN thread.

stories.title: Nvidia reports $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue in its first results under interim chief executive Colette Kress.
stories.summary: CBS News reports revenue of $115.8 billion for Nvidia's fiscal third quarter, against about $109 billion expected, and guidance of about $130 billion for the next quarter. Separately, the Financial Times reported that Nvidia no longer discloses its Singapore sales, which reached $104 billion in 2025.
stories.heat: HN 399 pts / 194 comments (Singapore disclosure story) · CBS News, CNBC, Quartz, Financial Times, Benzinga, TheStreet · velocity: high, results came out after the US close on 17 November
detail: Nvidia reported results for its fiscal third quarter after the US market closed on Tuesday 17 November. Revenue was $115.8 billion, up from $57 billion a year earlier, and analysts had expected nearly $109 billion (FactSet figure, reported by CBS News). Data centre revenue was a record $107.6 billion, up 110%. Profit was $65.3 billion, up 105%.

Nvidia expects about $130 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter. Shares rose nearly 4% to $161.57 in after-hours trading, CBS News reports. Before the results, CNBC reported that the stock had fallen for six weeks in a row, its longest losing run since 2012.

These are the first results since Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive on 12 November. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim chief executive. Board chair Harvey Jones said the company does not intend to reinstate Huang and that the board is considering internal and external candidates, according to CBS News. On Tuesday the board also formed a new committee on compliance with US export controls.

On the same day the Financial Times reported that Nvidia stopped disclosing its Singapore sales separately. Secondary reports of the FT article say company accounts show Nvidia's Singapore subsidiary booked $104 billion of external revenue in 2025, up 72%. Nvidia changed its geographic reporting from customer billing address to customer headquarters. Nvidia's earlier filings said customers use Singapore to centralise invoicing and that the products are almost always shipped elsewhere.

The change matters because of the US investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer suspected of diverting chips to China. Nvidia has said it has no evidence of diversion (CNBC). Kress said demand far exceeds supply and that the company will study the new US export rule issued on 16 November.
The FT article is paywalled and the Quartz and roic.ai pages refused automated access. The Singapore figures here come from search summaries of the FT report, not from the article itself.

stories.title: An internal update at Apple takes down iCloud sign-in, the App Store, Apple Pay and other services for several hours.
stories.summary: Apple said an internal update caused outages on 17 November and that it was not a cyberattack, 9to5Mac and Time report. Consumer services were back by the evening US time.
stories.heat: HN 631 pts / 352 comments, rank 3 of the day · Time, TechCrunch, 9to5Mac, Tom's Guide, Digital Trends · velocity: medium, peaked on 17 November and is now resolved for consumers
detail: Apple services failed for many users on Tuesday 17 November. 9to5Mac lists the App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay, Apple Support, iPhone activation and Apple Music, and says developers could not reach App Store Connect. Users were signed out of iCloud on iPhones and Macs and then could not sign back in.

Time reports that Apple's System Status page first showed an AppleCare outage at 11:15 a.m. Eastern Time, and that Downdetector had about 2,000 reports just before 1 p.m. An App Store outage was marked resolved by 3:30 p.m. and all services were listed as available by the evening.

Apple's statement, quoted by Time: "Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning." The company said the outage was not a cyberattack. 9to5Mac reported that developer services took longer to recover than consumer services.

A Hacker News commenter who visited an Apple shop said staff could not process orders or returns or activate new iPhones. That report is not confirmed by Apple. Apple's own status page returned no service data to an automated fetch.

stories.title: The NSA's classified internal network goes offline during maintenance, and officials say there is no sign of a cyberattack.
stories.summary: CBS News reports that NSANet went down on 17 November. The agency called it a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" and said critical capabilities kept working.
stories.heat: HN 474 pts / 549 comments · CNN (first report), CBS News, Reuters, Forbes, Scripps, WSJ via Jerusalem Post · velocity: high, restoration time was still unknown in the latest reports
detail: The National Security Agency's network for classified communications and information sharing, known as NSANet, went offline on Tuesday 17 November, CBS News reports, citing several US officials. CNN reported it first. It was not clear how long the network had been down or when full service would return.

The NSA called the event a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" and said "mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational". Two US officials told CBS News there was no evidence of a cyberattack. Two other sources said routine system patching caused the outage.

The agency staggered arrival times for non-emergency staff at its Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters, an arrangement sources called "Code Gray", so that large numbers of employees would not log on at once. Some activities moved to other NSA sites.

The outage came on the same day as the Apple outage. Hacker News commenters speculated about staff cuts, bad patches and attacks, with no evidence for any of them. The CNN page returned HTTP 451 to an automated fetch, so this account rests on CBS News.
stories.about: NSANet is the National Security Agency's internal network for classified work. It runs separately from the public internet.

stories.title: A Harvard study of 3.3 million pupils finds that strict smartphone bans in schools produce small gains in test scores.
stories.summary: The Associated Press reports that schools where phones are locked away all day gained the equivalent of one to two extra weeks of learning per year. A Stanford co-author of an earlier study calls the estimates small and sensitive.
stories.heat: HN 1168 pts / 582 comments, the day's top story · New York Times, Associated Press (KUER, Anchorage Daily News), SF Examiner · velocity: medium, published 17 November
detail: This is a study about a technology in schools: what happens to test scores when smartphones are removed for the whole school day. Harvard's Center for Education Policy Research, with professor Thomas Kane as a co-author, compared maths and reading scores for grades 4 to 10 over five school years, covering 3.3 million pupils at 4,600 US schools (Associated Press, carried by KUER).

Schools with strict rules, where pupils lock phones in pouches for the full day, were compared with similar schools without such rules. The gain was "modest": about one to two additional weeks of learning per school year, or roughly half of the yearly decline in scores seen since smartphones became common. Kane said the gains come gradually and that bans are "not a panacea".

A separate study in May, by researchers at Stanford, Michigan, Duke and Pennsylvania, found an overall effect "close to zero", with small gains in high-school maths over three years. Its co-author Thomas Dee told the AP that the Harvard estimates are small, sensitive and based on only a few years of bans, and called early results from both studies "largely disappointing".

More than 40 US states now restrict phones at school, the AP reports, but enforcement varies and pupils use workarounds such as second phones. The New York Times article and the Harvard page were blocked to automated fetch, so the figures here come from the AP report.

stories.title: Researchers disclose Java4Shell, a memory-corruption flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder that can allow remote code execution.
stories.summary: Security firm Calif says the flaw, rated 9.2 of 10, affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI. Calif says Oracle and OpenJDK released patches on 17 November.
stories.heat: HN 534 pts / 143 comments · Calif (the finder's own write-up) · velocity: high, disclosed 17 November with patches the same day
detail: Calif, a security research firm, published details on 17 November of a flaw it calls Java4Shell, which it lists as CVE-2026-114938 with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The bug is in the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder of OpenJDK. A malformed padded input makes the decoder write 64 bytes into a 50-byte buffer and corrupt nearby heap memory.

Calif says OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer is affected, with distributions built from it such as Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin and Oracle Java SE. Only x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI are affected (Intel Xeon Ice Lake and newer, AMD Zen 4 and newer). ARM64 is not affected.

According to Calif, the result can be a leak of memory or remote code execution. The firm reports working attacks against default set-ups of Keycloak, Jenkins, Confluence and Jira without a login, and against Kafka, Solr and Elasticsearch with a login. Each product needs its own attack chain, and Calif is holding those back until users have had time to update. Calif says it used AI tools in finding and exploiting the bug.

Calif says the OpenJDK advisory and Oracle's patch came out at 1:00 p.m. Pacific Time on 17 November. If you cannot patch at once, Calif gives two start-up options: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, or -XX:UseAVX=2 on x86-64 hosts only. This account rests on Calif's own page, and the Oracle and OpenJDK advisories were not read.
stories.about: Calif is a security research firm. OpenJDK is the open-source Java runtime on which most Java distributions are built.

stories.title: A new US rule requires licences for advanced AI chip sales to five more countries, and chip shares fall.
stories.summary: CyberScoop reports that the Commerce Department issued a 132-page interim final rule on 16 November covering Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. Yahoo Finance reports that AMD fell about 5% and Broadcom about 4% that day.
stories.heat: Not on the HN front page · CyberScoop, Yahoo Finance, CBS News, TradingKey, Stocktwits · velocity: medium, rule issued 16 November and Nvidia commented on it on 17 November
detail: The Bureau of Industry and Security, part of the US Commerce Department, issued a 132-page interim final rule on Monday 16 November. CyberScoop reports that it restricts exports of AI chips to overseas data centres in countries under US arms embargoes, a list of more than 20 countries that includes China, and requires new licences for advanced AI chip sales to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil.

Data centres, foreign foundries and chip exporters must check their customers, including indirect ownership by persons in countries of concern. Companies with pending or ongoing sales have 90 days to get the new licences. The "interim final" form lets Commerce skip the normal notice and comment period.

Chip shares fell on the day. Yahoo Finance reports AMD down about 5%, Broadcom about 4%, Micron and SK Hynix more than 7% each, and the PHLX Semiconductor Index more than 5%. Data-centre firms CoreWeave, Nebius and Supermicro each fell more than 6%.

The rule follows the US investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based buyer of Nvidia chips. Nvidia's interim chief executive Colette Kress said on 17 November that the company will study the rule, CBS News reports.

stories.title: Microsoft launches its own coding models, MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash, in GitHub Copilot.
stories.summary: Microsoft AI announced the two models at Ignite on 17 November. Microsoft claims MAI Code 2 reaches about 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at about 40% of the cost, on benchmarks Microsoft ran itself.
stories.heat: HN 288 pts / 135 comments · Microsoft AI (primary) · velocity: medium, launched 17 November on the same day as GPT-6.2
detail: Microsoft AI announced MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash on 17 November at its Ignite conference. MAI Code 2 is for enterprise coding work such as debugging, changes across many files and user-interface development. Flash is for high-volume routine work such as quick fixes and code explanations. Microsoft says neither model is tuned for science research or very long agentic tasks.

The performance figures are Microsoft's own claims. Microsoft ran the coding benchmarks on its internal MSBench platform with GitHub Copilot CLI, and says MAI Code 2 reached about 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at about 40% of the cost and about 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's performance at about 5% of the cost. It also says 258 annotators preferred MAI Code 2's front-end output over GPT-6 Sol's 64% of the time.

Both models are available in GitHub Copilot at a 50% promotional price, and Flash is in limited preview in Microsoft Foundry. Microsoft says a related model, MAI Work Flash, powers features in Excel, PowerPoint, Word and Teams.

stories.title: Uber is notifying nearly 150,000 people that hackers took their driving-licence details through its vendor Fireworks AI.
stories.summary: TechCrunch reports a total of 149,346 people from a filing with Oregon's attorney general. This is a new development in the Fireworks AI breach that the previous edition carried.
stories.heat: Not on the HN front page · TechCrunch, SecurityWeek, The Register · velocity: medium, the total became public on 16 November and The Register followed on 17 November
detail: What is new since the last edition: the size of the Uber part of the Fireworks AI breach. TechCrunch reported on 16 November that Uber has notified 149,346 people, a figure from a filing with Oregon's attorney general. The data taken includes names, addresses, dates of birth and driving-licence numbers.

Hackers broke into Fireworks AI in October and stole internal credentials, which they used to reach Uber's data. Fireworks told Uber on 9 October. Uber said its alerts for unauthorised access did not fire because the attackers used Fireworks' own credentials, and it referred further questions to Fireworks.

Fireworks attributed the breach to a financially motivated group that sells stolen access tokens for large language models. Notion and Cursor have also confirmed that data was stolen, TechCrunch reports. The Register notes that Uber has not said why licence data was held with an AI inference provider.
stories.about: Fireworks AI is a provider that lets developers run open-weight AI models through its service.

stories.title: Cloudflare warns that DNS provider Quad9's withdrawal from France shows the cost of court-ordered DNS blocking.
stories.summary: In a blog post, Cloudflare says the non-profit Quad9 is pulling its free DNS resolver out of France after a court ordered it to block domains under daily penalties. Cloudflare argues that a Belgian order with a January 2027 deadline raises the same risk.
stories.heat: HN 300 pts / 89 comments · Cloudflare blog (one source) · velocity: medium, posted in the window, the withdrawal itself was announced last month
detail: Cloudflare's post says Quad9, a Swiss non-profit, announced last month that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This followed months of litigation and a French court order to block domains linked to alleged copyright infringement, with daily financial penalties. The post does not give the penalty amounts or the exact date.

Cloudflare argues that DNS blocking does not work, because users can switch resolver and the content stays online, and that it blocks whole domains with no notice to the user. It notes that Cisco earlier withdrew OpenDNS from France and Portugal, and for a time from Belgium.

The post also says a Belgian court has ordered Cloudflare, Google and Cisco to start blocking through their public resolvers by early January 2027 or face penalties, and that all three have appealed. This is Cloudflare's account and Cloudflare is a party to the related cases. Quad9's own statement was not read.
stories.about: Quad9 is a Swiss non-profit that runs a free public DNS resolver (9.9.9.9) which blocks known malicious domains.

stories.title: A test of 22 coding-agent harnesses finds that the best-value harness changes from one AI model to the next.
stories.summary: Runta's FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 ran 27,280 trials across five open models and found the model explains 92.8% of cost differences. Runta sells an agent platform, and the results are its own.
stories.heat: HN 337 pts / 118 comments · Runta blog (one source) · velocity: medium, published 17 November
detail: Runta published the study on 17 November with inference provider Baseten. It ran 22 harness configurations on 5 open models (GLM-5.3, GLM Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Muse and Kimi-K3) over 62 terminal tasks, 4 attempts each: 27,280 runs and 83 billion tokens.

Results reported by Runta: the best-value harness was different for each model, and Codex CLI ranked 1st with GLM-5.3 but 16th with Kimi-K3. The model explained 92.8% of cost variance and the harness alone 2.3%. With the model fixed, the most expensive harness cost 1.8 to 5.0 times the cheapest. 64.5% of the cost went to trials that did not pass.

Limits stated in the post: only open models through one provider were tested, costs are list-price estimates, and each pass rate has a margin of about 10 points either way. Runta is a commercial company and the post promotes its platform.
stories.about: A harness is the software wrapped around an AI model that lets it act as a coding agent (examples: Codex CLI, OpenCode, Pi). Runta is an agent execution company.

stories.title: The hacker magazine Phrack publishes issue 73 with 23 papers, several of them on AI and exploitation.
stories.summary: Phrack's index dates the issue 17 November 2026. It includes a profile of Halvar Flake and papers on container escapes, kernel exploitation with language models and a Chromium sandbox escape.
stories.heat: HN 282 pts / 42 comments · Phrack (primary) · velocity: low, a release notice with a steady readership
detail: Phrack released issue 73 on 17 November 2026, according to its index. The issue has 23 main papers plus a profile of the researcher Halvar Flake and a history section with pieces on the 2000 SSH1 exploit and the 2003 Linux kernel backdoor attempt.

Papers include a Docker container escape through vDSO, a Chromium renderer sandbox escape through Skia, use-after-free exploitation in the Linux kernel, two WinFsp zero-days, and three on machine learning: a virus inside a language model, backdoor attacks on real machine-learning systems, and kernel exploit development with language models. The introduction says AI agents now analyse source code and reverse engineer binaries, and argues that human intuition becomes more valuable as execution gets cheaper.
stories.about: Phrack is an online hacker magazine first published in 1985. Its papers on exploitation techniques are widely read in the security field.

stories.title: Anthropic's Claude Code team describes how it checks code written by AI agents.
stories.summary: A post by Addy Osmani dated 16 November says about 90% of Claude Code's own code is written and reviewed by Claude, and sets out the tests and review rules the team uses. The figures are Anthropic's own.
stories.heat: HN 266 pts / 209 comments · claude.dev blog (primary) · velocity: low, published 16 November
detail: The post argues that verification is what lets a team run many coding agents at once: without reliable checks, a person must read every change. It recommends three kinds of test (end-to-end tests of real user flows, property tests and differential tests of old against new systems) and warns against flaky and slow tests.

Practices described: the agent runs the changed app and does not rely on tests alone, a failed check goes to a human after three fix attempts, review rules are read from the base branch so a change cannot alter its own checks, and a 39-item reliability checklist is applied per change. The post says a separate grader improved task success by up to 10 points in internal testing. These are the vendor's own figures.

stories.title: Microsoft's ONNX Runtime repository returns "not found" on GitHub, and Microsoft has given no explanation.
stories.summary: The repository github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime returned HTTP 404 when checked on 18 November. RuntimeWire reports at least seven related repositories are also gone, which breaks builds from source.
stories.heat: HN 127 pts / 32 comments, thread about two hours old at fetch time · RuntimeWire, GitHub issues in onnx/onnx and PyMuPDF · velocity: high, new and unexplained
detail: The main ONNX Runtime repository on GitHub returned HTTP 404 when fetched for this edition. An issue opened on 17 November in the separate onnx/onnx project says the repositories "have disappeared and this is breaking CI/CD systems", and names microsoft/onnxruntime and microsoft/onnxruntime-swift-package-manager. It had no reply from Microsoft.

RuntimeWire reported on 17 November that at least seven related repositories are missing and that release downloads fail, while the pip and NuGet packages still install. No statement from Microsoft or GitHub was found, and the cause is unknown. Guesses in the Hacker News thread (a security takedown, an attack) have no evidence behind them.
stories.about: ONNX Runtime is Microsoft's open-source engine for running machine-learning models in the ONNX format. Many applications and build pipelines depend on it.

stories.title: The JavaScript framework Solid reaches version 2.0 with async built into its reactive core.
stories.summary: Creator Ryan Carniato announced Solid 2.0 on 16 November after 23 release candidates. SolidStart is retired and several old APIs, including createResource, are removed.
stories.heat: HN 229 pts / 59 comments · SolidJS blog (primary) · velocity: low, a release notice
detail: Solid 2.0 was announced on 16 November 2026 by Ryan Carniato. Computations in the reactive graph can now return a Promise or an async iterator, with loading states handled by the framework. Server functions move into the core, and development builds report reactive mistakes with a stable code, a source location and a fix, a feature the post describes as aimed at coding agents.

The post says createResource, batch, startTransition, on, produce, createComputed and createMutable are "all gone", and that SolidStart is retired in favour of core primitives and Vite plugins. The team shipped 23 release candidates over 14 weeks, merged 971 pull requests and closed 753 issues before the stable release.
stories.about: Solid is an open-source JavaScript library for building user interfaces, known for fine-grained reactivity without a virtual DOM.

sections.title: Geopolitics
sections.blurb: Trump says Ukraine will come up in Shenzhen, the Quad voices concern about economic coercion in Manila, the United States loses its measles elimination status, and Mongolia's president announces his resignation.

stories.title: Trump says Ukraine will come up at Thursday's Shenzhen meeting with Xi and Putin, although his own officials said it was not on the agenda.
stories.summary: The first three-way meeting of the US, Chinese and Russian presidents is set for Thursday 19 November at Xi Jinping's state residence in Shenzhen. The Kremlin says Putin is '100% sure' to meet Trump separately, a meeting that was not on the White House schedule as of Tuesday (HNGN, TASS, DPA).
stories.heat: Live blogs at NBC, ABC and CNN; AP, Reuters, DPA, TASS, CNBC and Kyiv Independent all carrying previews; lead item in the 10 Things and Democracy Now digests of 17 Nov · velocity: high, the meeting is tomorrow and the agenda is still disputed
detail: What is new since the last edition: the 16 November edition reported that the White House had set the agenda as nuclear arms only. Since then Trump himself has contradicted that. Leaving the White House on Monday 16 November he said the three leaders would also discuss Ukraine, which he called his 'favourite subject', that Iran would come up 'a little bit', and that denuclearisation was a 'tough subject' (HNGN, 17 November). Senior US officials had told reporters that nuclear weapons would be the focus and that Russia's war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda (AP via PBS, 16 November).

The Kremlin describes a different meeting again. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told a Moscow briefing on 16 November that the trilateral will be held at the Chinese leader's state residence in Shenzhen, that its agenda is still being defined, and that Moscow expects a joint communique whose text is still being negotiated; if none is agreed, each leader will give his own assessment (TASS). He called the meeting a 'showstopper'. He also said Putin is '100% sure' to meet Trump one to one because both are at the APEC summit, that the time and venue are still being worked out, and that the Ukraine settlement and the American and Russian proposals for it are among the agreed topics. DPA noted that the White House's published schedule shows Trump meeting only Xi on Thursday.

China has confirmed the meeting but named no topics beyond world peace and stability among major powers. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said on 16 November that the meeting has 'groundbreaking significance' (AP, DPA). An unnamed senior Trump administration official played down expectations to DPA, saying Washington wants to discuss possible reductions in nuclear arsenals and sees this as a starting point.

The running order, as reported by HNGN, TASS and CNBC: Putin arrived in Shenzhen early on Wednesday 18 November and was due to hold a working breakfast with Xi the same day, where TASS said he would brief Xi on his recent contacts with the US, including the Abu Dhabi talks. Trump meets Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr in Manila on Wednesday and then flies to Shenzhen. On Thursday he has a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi, followed by the trilateral session. Trump also said in Manila that he would meet Putin 'if it's available' and that North Korea's Kim Jong Un 'would like to' meet; Beijing said it had no information about a Kim meeting (Philstar).

On the US and China track, CNBC reported that the one-year trade truce agreed in South Korea last year has been extended by two months to January 2027, that the two sides said in September they would lower tariffs on 30 billion dollars of goods without giving a date, and that US officials say Trump does not plan to raise Nvidia. Trump said he expects Xi to raise Taiwan (Philstar). No Ukrainian or European representative will be in Shenzhen; Ukraine's foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said in October that such a meeting would 'encourage Putin to continue this war' (Kyiv Independent).

Other leaders are using the summit too. Xi met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Shenzhen on Tuesday 17 November; China agreed to further tariff relief on about 400 million Canadian dollars of Canadian exports, including frozen pork, fish and seafood, and Canada extended tariff exemptions on some Chinese steel and aluminium by two years (AP via PBS). Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is expected at APEC on her first trip to China as prime minister (CNBC).

sources.name: AP via PBS NewsHour (Canada and China)

stories.title: In Manila, the Quad leaders voiced 'grave concerns' about economic coercion without naming China, and Trump signed a preliminary trade statement with Thailand.
stories.summary: Trump's first Quad leaders' meeting, on Tuesday 17 November, produced a joint statement against arbitrary export restrictions and what Trump called critical minerals agreements (Reuters, Al Jazeera). Separately, Thailand agreed in outline to drop tariffs on US exports and buy 2.6 billion dollars of US farm goods (ABC News).
stories.heat: Ground News: 16 sources on the Quad statement, flagged a Blindspot with 8% left coverage · Reuters, Al Jazeera, ABC live blog, SCMP, Philstar, Open magazine · velocity: high on Tuesday, now moving to the Marcos meeting and Shenzhen
detail: Trump landed in Manila at 5:33 pm local time on Tuesday 17 November and went straight to the Solaire Resort, where he met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi (ABC News). It was the first Quad leaders' meeting of his second term, and the first at leader level in two years according to the 10 Things digest.

The joint statement said the four 'strongly oppose' destabilising or unilateral actions that seek to change the status quo by force or coercion, and expressed 'grave concerns' about economic coercion, including arbitrary export restrictions (Reuters via Al-Monitor). It named no country. Al Jazeera noted that the US and Japan have both complained about China's rare earth export restrictions, and that China has in effect cut off key critical mineral exports to Japan for nearly a year.

Trump said the four had reached agreements to secure critical mineral supply chains that would prevent 'coercion by any single foreign supplier', and that the US would have 'everything we need' on rare earths in 10 months (Al Jazeera). No terms, companies or values were published. Philstar reported that the leaders also announced a 2027 exercise with P-8 and P-3C maritime patrol aircraft, continued work on an AI accelerator for the Indo-Pacific, and a first Quad Business Leaders' Forum in 2027.

On the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN Summit, Trump and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul signed a joint statement on reciprocal trade. It sets out proposed terms, not a final deal. Trump said Thailand would remove all tariffs on US exports, lift non-tariff barriers on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry, and buy 2.6 billion dollars of US agricultural products, with a formal agreement 'in the coming weeks'; Anutin said 'still more' work remained (ABC News).

At the US and ASEAN special summit Trump told leaders 'We're with you always' and urged cooperation on critical minerals, rare earths and magnets; the US and ASEAN also finalised principles on fighting online scams (Philstar). Protesters in Manila called for scrapping Pax Silica, the US-led supply chain initiative (Philstar). On Wednesday 18 November Trump was due to hold a formal bilateral with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr before flying to Shenzhen; Philstar reported that the presidential palace said Marcos would seek a cut to the US tariff on Philippine exports, and Reuters reported he would press for stronger US security commitments in the South China Sea. No outcome of that meeting had been reported when this edition closed.

sources.name: Reuters via Yahoo News (Marcos meeting preview)

stories.title: The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, which it had held since 2000, along with Mexico and Bolivia.
stories.summary: The Pan American Health Organization announced the decision on Tuesday 17 November; the CDC counts 5,412 US infections this year (ABC News). A day earlier, CDC scientists reported 13 babies born with measles and 112 confirmed cases in pregnant women (AP via NBC News).
stories.heat: Ground News Daily Briefing item on the 13 congenital cases (18 Nov) · AP, ABC News, CNN, The Hill, Stateline, PBS, AFP via France 24 · velocity: high, the PAHO ruling landed on 17 Nov on top of the congenital-cases report of 16 Nov
detail: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization's office for the Americas, announced on Tuesday 17 November that the United States no longer holds measles elimination status. A country loses the status when the same strain of the virus has circulated for 12 months or more. The US was first declared measles-free in 2000 (ABC News). The same ruling covered Mexico and Bolivia, according to AFP as cited by Wikipedia's current events page and other outlets; Canada lost its status a year ago.

The numbers, from ABC News citing CDC data: 5,412 infections this year in nearly every state, 48 outbreaks, and 10 deaths reported by state health departments. The US used to average about 180 cases a year and had under 300 in 2024. Large outbreaks are continuing in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Minnesota and Indiana, and New York State has declared a state of emergency. MMR coverage among kindergarteners fell from 95% in 2019-20 to 92% in 2025-26; 95% is the level at which outbreaks are considered unlikely.

On Monday 16 November, CDC scientists published a public health alert in NEJM Evidence, with the University of Minnesota's Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy, reporting 13 cases of congenital measles (a baby infected in the womb) and 112 confirmed measles cases during pregnancy since the start of 2025. Almost all the women were unvaccinated or of unknown vaccination status (AP via NBC News). Michael Osterholm, who directs the Minnesota centre, said: 'This is a brand new phenomenon.' The MMR vaccine cannot be given during pregnancy.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr wrote on X that the government would 'work to regain U.S. measles elimination status' and said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said 'The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does' (ABC News). Medical organisations, which have sued over the reduced childhood vaccine schedule introduced under Kennedy, blame vaccine misinformation for the fall in coverage (ABC News).

stories.title: Four days after the nationwide US ground stop, the Transportation Secretary asked senators for 50 billion dollars and said the root cause is still not clear.
stories.summary: Sean Duffy raised the air traffic control request from 30 billion to about 50 billion dollars at a Senate Republican lunch on Tuesday 17 November and met scepticism (CBS News). The 13 Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee demanded technical briefings, and the FAA halted installation of the router type involved (ABC News).
stories.heat: Ground News Daily Briefing item 'GAO warned FAA before grounding' (18 Nov) · CBS, ABC, CNN, NBC, Washington Post, Al Jazeera, Democracy Now · velocity: medium to high, the outage was on 13 Nov but the funding fight and the blame dispute are growing
detail: The Federal Aviation Administration stopped all departures nationwide for nearly five hours on Friday 13 November after a telecommunications failure. Democracy Now, as carried by Havana Times, put the damage at more than 18,000 cancellations and more than 28,000 delays and called it the largest US air disruption since 11 September 2001.

On Tuesday 17 November Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford went to the Senate. Duffy asked for 50.1 billion dollars to rebuild air traffic control, 20 billion more than the request sent on 12 November, on top of 12.5 billion already appropriated (ABC News). He said he had 'decided to put everything on the table' (CBS News). Republican reactions were mixed: Senator John Kennedy said he was furious about the jump, Senator Rick Scott backed about 10 billion with airlines paying a share, Senator Eric Schmitt supported the full amount, and Majority Leader John Thune said the path forward 'remains to be seen' (CBS News).

Duffy's account of the cause, as reported by ABC News: contractors were replacing copper wire with fibre in El Dorado, Arkansas, and when a router there was switched on, a system in Amarillo, Texas, replaced about three weeks earlier, began to flood the network. He told senators the department had been able to recreate what happened but 'the root cause of what happened, we don't have clarity yet' (US Department of Transportation). Common Dreams reported that air traffic controllers dispute his explanation.

The 13 Commerce Committee Democrats wrote to Duffy and Bedford on Tuesday asking for the root cause, an explanation of why the network lacked redundancy, technical briefings from the FAA and the contractors L3Harris and Juniper by Monday, and a pause on installing more Juniper devices. The FAA said the same day that it was halting Juniper router installation (ABC News).

The warnings in the Ground News headline: a Government Accountability Office report in September on the FAA's accelerated rebuild said the agency 'could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions', and CNN reported on 16 November that the FAA had fielded years of warnings about ageing systems (search summaries of CNN and Aerocorner; the CNN page itself could not be opened for this edition). Trump said on Monday that Duffy is 'doing a great job' (ABC News).

stories.title: China threatens countermeasures after a new US rule requires licences for advanced AI chips sent to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
stories.summary: China's Commerce Ministry declared 'firm opposition' on Tuesday 17 November to the rule the US published a day earlier, two days before Trump meets Xi (AFP). Malaysia's trade minister said it will not negotiate with Washington over the rule and expects data centre operators to comply (search summary of regional reports).
stories.heat: Ground News Daily Briefing item 'US limits overseas AI chip access' (18 Nov) · UPI, Fortune, AFP, Quartz, CNBC · velocity: medium to high, the reactions arrived on 17 Nov and the rule lands in the middle of the Asia trip
detail: The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security released an interim final rule on Monday 16 November. It requires a US licence for data centres anywhere in the world that provide large amounts of computing power from advanced AI chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau and other restricted places, and a licence to export advanced chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the rule says 'present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion' (UPI). It takes effect on publication in the Federal Register; data centres already serving such customers get 90 days to obtain a licence, and US-headquartered operators have a carve-out (Fortune).

The diplomatic effect is the news in the window. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on Tuesday that the US 'repeatedly overstretches the concept of national security' and that China would 'take necessary measures'. The Commerce Ministry said late on Tuesday that it firmly opposed the curbs and threatened countermeasures, without naming any (AFP via Insider Paper). US officials say Trump does not plan to raise the Nvidia affair with Xi on Thursday (CNBC).

Three of the five named countries were at the table with Trump in Manila on Tuesday, and Thailand signed a trade statement with him the same day. According to a search summary of regional reports, Malaysia's Trade Minister Johari Abdul Ghani said Kuala Lumpur does not intend to negotiate over the rule and expects operators to abide by it, and Singapore said it is studying the measure and talking to affected companies. These two reactions were not read on a primary page for this edition. Fortune quoted analyst Joshua Kurlantzick as saying the controls could be 'disastrous' for Malaysia's plan to be a data centre hub.

stories.title: Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands plan to send rejected asylum seekers to a return hub in Rwanda from next year.
stories.summary: The five governments are negotiating with Kigali over what would be the EU's first return hub, a pilot for about 100 people at a time (Reuters). No agreement has been signed, and it is unclear whether the plan would survive European court review.
stories.heat: Reuters explainer, AFP, AP, SCMP; item 9 in the 10 Things digest of 17 Nov; one aggregator counted 11 outlets · velocity: medium, announced this week with talks ongoing
detail: The plan covers adults who have exhausted every legal route to stay in the EU but cannot be sent home, for example because their country refuses them or is considered unsafe. They would spend a few weeks in language and skills training at the hub and then settle in Rwanda, or return to their home country instead (Reuters). The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said it differs from Britain's abandoned scheme, which would have sent people to Rwanda while their claims were still being processed.

Scale is small: about 100 people at a time, a few hundred a year, against 669,365 asylum applications in the EU last year (Reuters). AFP's diplomatic sources said each country would send about 20 people in the pilot. The five say they are using a new EU framework that permits return hubs in third countries. Cost and what Rwanda receives are not settled; Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said Rwanda is not seeking payment.

The main legal dispute is whether the EU's responsibility ends at transfer. The EU Agency for Fundamental Rights says member states stay accountable for rights violations afterwards. The Council of Europe and UN rights chief Volker Turk have voiced concern, and Human Rights Watch pointed to Rwanda's record of repressing dissent. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the hub a potential game changer (10 Things, citing SCMP and AFP), while Austria's far-right Freedom Party called it 'worthless' (Reuters).

stories.title: The EU's climate envoy says the first draft of the COP31 deal could make the Antalya talks 'untenable', three days before the deadline.
stories.summary: Australia, which leads the negotiations, published an 18-page draft on Monday 16 November that calls for a fossil fuel phase-out and for rich countries to reach net zero by 2030 (AFP). Climate Minister Chris Bowen said there may be 'at least one more draft' before the talks are due to end on Friday 20 November.
stories.heat: Reuters, AFP, Al Jazeera, ABC Australia, Carbon Brief tracker · velocity: medium, rising towards Friday's deadline
detail: What is new since the last edition, which reported COP31 entering its final week: the first draft of the cover decision is out, and it has split the room. The 18-page text published on Monday 16 November includes calls for a phase-out of fossil fuels, wording that oil-producing states have long resisted, and for wealthy nations to reach net zero emissions by 2030 (AFP via Yahoo News, 17 November). A search summary of the Reuters report says it also proposes tripling adaptation finance to at least 120 billion dollars.

EU climate envoy Wopke Hoekstra said the draft 'needs significant change'. An unnamed European official told AFP that emerging countries were trying to load obligations on developed nations as a tactic, and pointed to a bloc including Saudi Arabia and India. Brazil's environment minister Joao Paulo Capobianco said deadlocks can be eased by changing the wording. Antigua and Barbuda's environment minister said agreement on net zero could be very difficult but that he wants a commitment to phase out fossil fuels.

A second fight is over climate science. Dozens of European, African and Pacific states want the IPCC's next assessment reports published before COP33 in 2028. Saudi Arabia, at the centre of the dispute, said on Tuesday that it is 'not seeking to delay climate science' but did not say when it wants the reports out (AFP). COP decisions need consensus, so one country can block the outcome, and these talks often run past their deadline.

stories.title: Mongolia's President Ukhnaa Khurelsukh has announced his resignation, a day after the opposition accused him of taking bribes over a railway contract.
stories.summary: Khurelsukh denies wrongdoing and says he will cooperate with investigators; parliament must accept the resignation and is expected to vote this week (AP and Reuters reports, via search summaries). If it does, the speaker becomes interim president and an election follows within four months.
stories.heat: AP, Reuters, Bloomberg, AFP, Anadolu, ITV · velocity: medium, announced 17 Nov with a parliamentary vote still to come
detail: Khurelsukh announced on Tuesday 17 November that he would step down. On Monday the opposition Democratic Party had accused several senior officials, including the president, of corruption, and demanded that he resign or face impeachment. The allegation is that he made sure a railway contract went in 2019 to Bodi International, one of the country's largest conglomerates, without a competitive tender, and took bribes from the company. He said the claims were meant to 'defame and insult' the president. Local reports said the justice minister and his deputy also resigned.

Under Mongolian law the 126-member State Great Khural must approve the resignation. If it does, the speaker serves as interim president and a presidential election must be held within four months. The country has had months of political turmoil: in March lawmakers appointed the third prime minister in under 12 months after weeks of anti-corruption protests. These details come from search summaries of the AP, Reuters and Bloomberg reports; the AP page itself could not be opened for this edition.
stories.about: Ukhnaa Khurelsukh, a former prime minister from the ruling Mongolian People's Party, has been president of Mongolia since 2021. The State Great Khural is the country's single-chamber parliament.

stories.title: Turkish police raided the pro-opposition channel Sozcu TV in Istanbul, took it off air and put it under a state-appointed trustee.
stories.summary: Four executives were detained in the raid early on Tuesday 17 November, and prosecutors accuse the channel's owner of leading a terrorist organisation linked to the Gulen network (Hurriyet Daily News). It is the second opposition broadcaster placed under a trustee in five weeks, after Halk TV on 14 October.
stories.heat: Reuters, Hurriyet Daily News, Bianet, DPA, Democracy Now · velocity: medium, one-day event with opposition reaction
detail: Police cordoned off and searched Sozcu TV's headquarters in Istanbul's Sariyer district. The Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) was appointed trustee of the channel and its news website; the group's print newspapers were not affected (Hurriyet Daily News, Reuters as summarised in search). Those detained include the board chair and a former general manager.

The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office said it is investigating owner Burak Akbay for 'establishing or managing a terrorist organisation' and for propaganda, alleging he set up the outlets to serve the network of the late cleric Fethullah Gulen and financed related companies through overseas accounts, citing reports from the financial crimes board MASAK. The channel's lawyer said the allegations were revived after an appeals court overturned a ruling in an earlier case, and that no offence had been established in that file.

Ozgur Ozel, leader of the main opposition CHP, said the move showed the government had 'no tolerance for even the smallest criticism' (Reuters, via search summary). Halk TV, another opposition-leaning broadcaster, was put under trustees on 14 October in a separate corruption investigation and its news website has stopped publishing (Hurriyet Daily News).
stories.about: Sozcu is a Turkish secular-nationalist media group critical of President Erdogan's government; its television channel launched in 2023. TMSF is the state deposit insurance fund that Turkish courts appoint to run seized companies.

sections.title: Krieg
sections.blurb: A span of the Crimean Bridge collapses, Russia fires ballistic missiles at Kyiv's bridges, Iran and the US trade strikes over Bahrain and Qeshm, and Saudi-backed forces reinforce the road to Aden.

stories.title: A road span and an arch of the Crimean Bridge collapsed after a second night of Ukrainian strikes, Ukraine's General Staff says.
stories.summary: Ukraine's General Staff said the road link between Russia and occupied Crimea was cut on the night of 16 to 17 November; Zelensky called it the last stage of a seven-stage operation (AP via PBS). Russia confirmed drone damage and a halt to road traffic, and said the bridge will be restored.
stories.heat: Lead item on 10 Things and the Democracy Now digest · AP/PBS, ABC News, CNN, NPR, BBC, Guardian, Kyiv Independent (five follow-up pieces) · velocity: high, second raid in two nights and the damage was confirmed on 17 Nov
detail: New since the last edition: the 16 November edition carried the first raid on the bridge. On the night of 16 to 17 November Ukraine struck it again, and this time Ukraine's General Staff said an arch and a span of the road section collapsed, which cut the road link. The rail line still stands, but one of its arches is damaged, the General Staff said (AP via PBS).

President Volodymyr Zelensky called the operation "unprecedented" and described seven stages over several weeks, in which Ukrainian forces first knocked out Russian air defences, radars and electronic warfare equipment on the route to the bridge. In the final stage, he said, Ukrainian long-range drones hit the road section, Neptune missiles and other drones hit the rail section, and Flamingo cruise missiles delivered the final blow. Fire Point, the maker of the Flamingo, said about 900 feet of road surface was destroyed and one of the two arches fell (ABC News). Videos published by Ukraine show part of the deck in the water; AP said it could not verify them.

Russia's account is narrower. Its Investigative Committee said the bridge was hit by drones and damaged, and opened a terrorism case. Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-appointed head of Crimea, said road traffic was halted and that rail traffic resumed by Tuesday afternoon; he did not describe the damage. He also said two people were killed in a drone attack in the Lenin district near Kerch (ABC News). Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge will be restored and will be better than before.

Russia's Defence Ministry said it shot down 1,441 Ukrainian drones overnight, after 1,336 the night before. Moscow's mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, said about 800 drones flew toward the Moscow region and 321 were shot down near the capital. All four Moscow airports had temporary flight restrictions (ABC News). Authorities in Bashkortostan said they repelled a "massive" drone attack on industrial zones in Ufa and Salavat; the independent outlet Astra reported a large fire at the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat complex, about 1,300 km from the Ukrainian border (AP via PBS).

Why it matters: the road and rail bridge, opened by Vladimir Putin after the 2014 annexation, is a main supply route for Russian units and bases in Crimea. Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara called the strike a direct response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian bridges (Kyiv Independent). Putin made no public comment before he left for China, where he is due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping on Thursday 19 November.

stories.title: Iran launched drones at a US radar in Bahrain for the third time in five days, and the US answered with a strike on Qeshm Island.
stories.summary: The IRGC said on 17 November that it hit the US-run radar at Sheikh Isa air base; CENTCOM said every drone was intercepted with no damage (Al Jazeera, AP). Hours later a US jet struck an IRGC missile launch site on Qeshm, and Kuwait's army said it was under drone attack.
stories.heat: Top item in the Democracy Now digest and the AP Mideast round-up · AP (KPBS), Al Jazeera, The Hill, Iran International, Washington Post · velocity: high, strikes in both directions on the same day after a two-month lull
detail: New since the last edition: the 16 November edition carried the 15 November drone attack at Riffa. On Tuesday 17 November Iran attacked Bahrain a third time, the US struck Iranian territory in reply, and Kuwait reported drones over its own territory.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) said it carried out a "precision operation" with drones against the US-operated radar at Sheikh Isa air base, in answer to "repeated violations of Iranian airspace by US military drones" and to US strikes on Iranian communications towers. US Central Command said the drones "were intercepted without any damage to US equipment or personnel" and rejected the claim of a hit. Bahrain said its air defences stopped the attack; blasts were heard over Manama, and Bahrain's Interior Ministry issued three security alerts in under 24 hours (Al Jazeera, Iran International). Neither side reported casualties.

Hours later a US fighter jet struck an IRGC missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz with "precision munitions", an unnamed US official told AP. Iran's state agency IRNA reported five to six explosions. Ahmad Nafisi, deputy governor of Hormozgan province, said there was no damage to homes, businesses or infrastructure.

Kuwait's army said on Tuesday night that the country was under "hostile drone attacks" and that the explosions heard were interceptions. It did not say where the drones came from and reported no casualties or damage (Al Jazeera).

The exchange ends a lull of about two months in a war that began on 28 February. The USS Theodore Roosevelt strike group arrived on Monday, joining the carriers George H.W. Bush and George Washington, so US naval strength in the region is now above its level at the start of the war (AP). Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE condemned the attack on Bahrain. Qatar, which is mediating, said the attacks "undermine diplomatic efforts". Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi met Oman's foreign minister in Muscat on shipping and diplomatic options.

Analysts quoted by AP read the attacks as pressure against the US naval blockade. Sascha Bruchmann of the International Institute for Strategic Studies said Tehran is growing impatient as its economy worsens, and that the Bahrain attacks are not decisive: "This is not it, yet."

stories.title: Iran denies a CNN report that US intelligence sees Tehran weighing a dirty bomb or chemical attack on officials in Washington.
stories.summary: CNN, citing seven US officials, reported on 16 November that Iran was developing options against senior Trump administration officials; the White House said there is no credible threat to the homeland. On 17 November Iran's foreign minister called the report "RUBBISH" and Trump warned of unprecedented consequences.
stories.heat: 10 Things item 3 · CNN (origin), Al Jazeera explainer, Time, Fox News, Times of India, Outlook India · velocity: high, denials and Trump's warning came on 17 Nov
detail: New: a threat story that both governments answered on 17 November. CNN reported on Monday 16 November, citing seven US officials, that intelligence indicates Iran is developing options to attack senior Trump administration officials in Washington, possibly with a radioactive dirty bomb or a chemical weapon. The officials said there is no evidence that Tehran has decided to act or has the people in place to do it. One source described intercepted Iranian "chatter" that bomb-making material was already inside the US; officials disagree on whether that is credible (CNN, as summarised by 10 Things and Al Jazeera).

The White House said there are currently no credible threats to the US homeland. On Tuesday Trump said Iran would face unprecedented consequences if it threatened Washington and that the administration was looking into the report. Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi called the report "RUBBISH" and blamed Israel for it, without giving evidence. Deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi called it a "shameful lie" (Iran International), and Iran's UN mission denied the chemical weapons allegation.
The story rests on unnamed US officials and one outlet's reporting; no independent confirmation exists. Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera called a dirty bomb attack highly unlikely.
stories.about: A dirty bomb is a conventional explosive packed with radioactive material. It spreads contamination and fear; it is not a nuclear weapon and causes no nuclear blast.

stories.title: Seven Russian ballistic missiles were fired at two of Kyiv's Dnipro bridges, Zelensky says, and both bridges were closed.
stories.summary: Zelensky said four missiles targeted the Southern bridge and three the Northern bridge on the night of 16 to 17 November; Ukraine's emergency service reported two dead in Kyiv (Kyiv Independent). Power failed for 700,000 households in Dnipropetrovsk region, according to the energy company DTEK.
stories.heat: Kyiv Independent, Kyiv Post, AP/PBS, ABC News, NPR, United24 · velocity: high, same night as the Crimean Bridge strike and described by Kyiv as its trigger
detail: New since the last edition: Russia hit transport crossings inside the capital. Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed strikes on the Northern (Pivnichnyi) and Southern (Pivdennyi) bridges over the Dnipro. Zelensky said four ballistic missiles targeted the Southern bridge and three the Northern one; he did not say how many hit. Both were closed for inspection, and by about 4 p.m. traffic had partly resumed on the Southern bridge in one direction for lighter vehicles (Kyiv Independent).

Ukraine's State Emergency Service said two people were killed in Kyiv's Obolonskyi district; it was not clear whether they died in the missile strike or in a later drone alert. Klitschko reported damage to critical infrastructure with water and heating cuts in some areas.

Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 306 drones, 92 of them jet-powered, plus ballistic and cruise missiles, and that 205 drones and six missiles were shot down or suppressed, with hits at 44 places (ABC News). Casualty counts differ by source: in Zaporizhzhia region the acting governor reported two dead and 31 injured (Kyiv Independent), while AP gave two dead and 18 wounded; ABC News, citing local officials, also reported at least three dead in Chernihiv and one in Vinnytsia. DTEK said 700,000 households in Dnipropetrovsk region lost power.

Russia's Defence Ministry said it hit military industry, energy, transport and port sites, and cargo ships in Odesa region. Poland activated air defence forces during the attack (ABC News). Ukraine Business News reported a government plan for eight temporary Dnipro crossings in Kyiv at about 12.3 billion hryvnias ($275 million).

stories.title: The LPG tanker Tara Gas was hit a second time near the Strait of Hormuz and one Indian sailor is missing, India's shipping minister says.
stories.summary: The Panama-flagged Tara Gas was struck on 16 November off Khasab, Oman, and again on 17 November, after which its 25 crew abandoned ship (Gulf News, gCaptain). Iran says tankers are hitting mines; Brent crude held near $93 (OilPrice.com).
stories.heat: Gulf News, gCaptain, The Wire, Riviera, Seatrade, Al Jazeera, OilPrice · velocity: high, second strike and a missing sailor on 17 Nov, further mine claims from Iran the same day
detail: New since the last edition, which carried one tanker hit in Hormuz: the Tara Gas was hit twice in two days and a crew member is now missing. The first strike, on Monday 16 November about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, disabled the ship and started an engine-room fire, according to the security firm Vanguard and the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency. India's ports and shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal first said all 25 crew (24 of them Indian by Al Jazeera's account) were safe.

On Tuesday 17 November the ship was hit again and the crew abandoned it. Sonowal then said: "While 24 crew members have been safely accounted for, one Indian seafarer remains missing." gCaptain and The Wire reported two other crew injured. India's foreign ministry said the other Indian crew were brought ashore at Khasab, and India condemned the attack.

The cause is disputed. Indian officials first described a missile attack. Iranian media carried the IRGC Navy's statement that the vessel struck a naval mine. No independent body has confirmed either account. Iran's armed forces said three tankers struck mines in the strait on Tuesday, and Iran's Navy later spoke of a fourth in 24 hours (Al Jazeera, The New Arab). The US military says it has cleared the main routes of mines. A second Panama-flagged ship, the On Phoenix, was hit by an unidentified projectile off Oman on Monday (Al Jazeera).

Oil: Brent traded near $93 a barrel on 17 November, held in place by tanker attacks on one side and recovering Gulf exports on the other (OilPrice.com). AP reports that escorted tankers have brought Gulf shipments back to roughly pre-war levels. Iraq restarted its pipeline to Turkey's Ceyhan port at 120,000 barrels a day, with a target of 500,000, to depend less on Hormuz (AP).

stories.title: Saudi-backed forces reinforced Tur al-Baha, 85 km from Aden, a day after Riyadh replaced its coalition commander in Yemen.
stories.summary: Two Yemeni military officials told AP that troops and equipment went to Tur al-Baha on 17 November ahead of an expected Houthi offensive. The Houthi health ministry said a strike on a factory in Hodeida killed at least seven; the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed 60 Houthi targets.
stories.heat: 10 Things item 4 (BBC, Guardian) · AP/Washington Post, Al Jazeera, Al-Monitor, Middle East Eye, The New Arab, Politics Today · velocity: medium to high, front still moving and a command change on 16 Nov
detail: New since the last edition, which carried the Houthi push to Khor Omairah: on Monday 16 November King Salman removed Lt. Gen. Fahd bin Hamad Al-Salman as commander of the coalition's Joint Forces and gave the post to the chief of the general staff, Gen. Fayyad Al-Ruwaili (Saudi Press Agency, via Al-Monitor). Two Western diplomats linked the change to the weekend's rapid losses (Politics Today, citing CNN). On Tuesday 17 November government forces sent more troops and equipment to Tur al-Baha, about 85 km from Aden, which they call the city's first line of defence (AP).

The Houthis now hold the Bab el-Mandeb coast after government forces withdrew to defend Aden. Estimates of the distance to Aden vary: about 100 km at Khor Omairah (Reuters), about 60 km to the northwest (AFP), about 70 km from Aden's northern entrance (Middle East Eye). The Houthis have said repeatedly that they will not attack Aden (AP).

Each side gave its own figures. Yemen's army spokesman Col. Majed al-Nuzaili said on Monday that the army made 661 attacks under its "Dawn of Yemen" offensive, which began on 5 October, and killed or wounded 173 Houthi fighters (Al Jazeera). Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said 60 Houthi targets were destroyed in four provinces (Iran International). The Houthi health ministry said a strike on a sponge factory in Hodeida killed at least seven people and wounded nine, and that two more died in Saada province; Houthi media blamed Saudi Arabia for strikes on Sanaa on Tuesday evening. AP could not verify the claims and Riyadh did not comment.

Yemen's parliament voted unanimously to name the Houthis a terrorist organisation; the bill goes to Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Presidential Leadership Council (Al Jazeera). The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted Houthi drones over Riyadh and Mecca provinces on Monday (Al-Monitor).
stories.about: Tur al-Baha is a district town in Lahij province on the road from Taiz to Aden. Aden has been the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government since the Houthis took Sanaa.

stories.title: The Abu Dhabi talks between Ukraine and Russia ended without a ceasefire, and Zelensky announced a meeting with US and European allies in Berlin.
stories.summary: The one concrete result of Abu Dhabi was a planned prisoner exchange of up to 1,300 people, Zelensky said (Kyiv Independent, 17 November). The Berlin meeting may fall on 19 November, the day Trump, Putin and Xi are due to meet in China.
stories.heat: Kyiv Independent, AP/PBS; Trump, Putin and Xi summit coverage across outlets · velocity: medium, talks stalled but two meetings are set for 19 Nov
detail: New since the last edition, which carried EU ministers on talks with Russia: the US-brokered round in Abu Dhabi ended without a ceasefire breakthrough. Zelensky said the only concrete outcome is a prisoner-of-war exchange that could cover up to 1,300 people. On 17 November he said US envoys, Ukrainian officials and European allies will meet in Berlin this week to agree positions; a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent it could be on 19 November, when Chancellor Friedrich Merz hosts a Coalition of the Willing summit.

Ukrainian, US and European teams held a video call on Monday with US envoys Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and Alexus Grynkewich (AP). Kushner said Moscow is open to European countries joining the negotiations, which the Kyiv Independent describes as a change in the Kremlin's position. Territory remains the block: Russia demands the parts of Donetsk and Luhansk regions it has not captured, and Kyiv refuses. Zelensky also said Ukraine has proposed humanitarian pauses, like the earlier one in Oleshky, in ten more occupied settlements.

stories.title: Japan scrambled fighters and protested to Moscow after two suspected Russian military aircraft entered its airspace near Okinoshima.
stories.summary: Tokyo said each aircraft was over Japanese territorial waters for about three minutes shortly after 4 a.m. on 17 November (Japan Times, AFP via Kuwait Times). South Korea separately sent up fighters when Russian aircraft entered its air defence identification zone, and said they did not enter Korean airspace.
stories.heat: 10 Things (Japan Times, Chosun) · AFP via The Standard and Kuwait Times, TRT World, Manila Times, Interfax-Ukraine · velocity: medium, one incident with a formal protest
detail: New, not in the last edition. Japan's government said two suspected Russian military aircraft entered Japanese airspace near Okinoshima shortly after 4 a.m. local time on Tuesday 17 November, each for about three minutes. Japan scrambled fighters to warn them and lodged a protest with Moscow. The aircraft reportedly passed through the Tsushima Strait and later flew between Yonaguni and Taiwan into the Pacific.

South Korea said it deployed fighters and carried out tactical manoeuvres after several Russian military aircraft entered and left its air defence identification zone; they did not enter South Korean airspace. Such a zone is a buffer for identifying aircraft, not sovereign airspace. The search results describe the last comparable protest by Japan as 2024, when a Russian patrol plane entered its airspace three times. No Russian government response was found.
stories.about: Okinoshima is a small Japanese island in the sea between Kyushu and the Korean peninsula, north of Fukuoka.

stories.title: Israeli fire killed at least four Palestinians in Gaza on 17 November, among them a 6-year-old boy, medics told Reuters.
stories.summary: Medics said gunfire killed two people in eastern Deir al-Balah and airstrikes killed two more in Khan Younis and Bir al-Naja (Reuters). Xinhua, citing Palestinian medical sources, put the day's toll at six; the Israeli military did not immediately comment.
stories.heat: Reuters (US News, Yahoo, regional syndication), Xinhua, Democracy Now digest · velocity: medium, daily deaths under a ceasefire that is 13 months old
detail: New since the last edition, which carried the killing of the Rafah brigade commander: on Tuesday 17 November medics said Israeli gunfire killed two people, one of them a 6-year-old boy, in separate incidents in eastern Deir al-Balah, and that airstrikes killed two more in Khan Younis and Bir al-Naja (Reuters). Xinhua, citing Palestinian medical sources, reported six dead. The Israeli military did not immediately comment on the incidents.

Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the October 2025 ceasefire took effect, and more than 74,000 since October 2023. UN spokesperson Farhan Haq said an Israeli airstrike hit very close to a UN-led fuel convoy in Rafah. Haaretz reported data showing Israel has not met its aid commitments under the ceasefire, with food deliveries falling (both via the Democracy Now digest in Havana Times). No new Lebanon strike was found after the 16 November Janta strike that the last edition carried.

stories.title: Norway, Sweden, Germany and Britain pledged new weapons money for Ukraine at the Ukraine Defense Contact Group on 17 November.
stories.summary: Norway gave $300 million and Germany $300 million to NATO's PURL fund for US weapons; Sweden gave 720 million kronor (about $71 million), and Britain announced a £240 million air defence package with more than 1,000 short-range missiles (Kyiv Independent).
stories.heat: Kyiv Independent (three pieces), AP/PBS · velocity: medium, pledges announced on the day Kyiv's bridges were hit
detail: New, 17 November: at the 37th meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, Norway pledged $300 million to NATO's Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), which pays for US weapons for Ukraine. Sweden pledged 720 million kronor (about $71 million), of which 200 million goes to PURL and 180 million to the Czech-led ammunition purchase. Germany's defence minister Boris Pistorius announced $300 million for PURL the same day. Norway and Sweden together come to about $371 million.

Britain announced £240 million ($317 million) in air defence support for this winter, with more than 1,000 short-range missiles and over a dozen radars (AP). Ukraine has an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors, its main defence against ballistic missiles, and the Kyiv Independent says the global shortage has grown since the US went to war with Iran. Zelensky asked allies for 40 more F-16s.
stories.about: PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) is a NATO mechanism through which European allies pay for US-made weapons that are then sent to Ukraine.

stories.title: Seven drones crossed into Moldova during Russia's 17 November attack on Ukraine, and one flew over Chisinau, Moldova's Defence Ministry says.
stories.summary: Five drones crashed near Moldovan villages, one of them about 10.7 km from the capital, and no one was hurt (Kyiv Independent, citing the ministry). President Maia Sandu said Moldova lacks the means to defend itself against drones.
stories.heat: Kyiv Independent, citing Moldova's Defence Ministry · velocity: medium, incursions are becoming more frequent (23 Oct, 12 Nov, 17 Nov)
detail: New, 17 November: Moldova's Defence Ministry said seven drones entered its airspace during the Russian mass attack on Ukraine. A Shahed-type drone was seen over Chisinau. Five crashed near the villages of Cheltuitori, Pohorniceni, Pohrebeni, Cuhurestii de Jos and Baxani, a sixth impact was possible in Ocnita district, and the seventh was lost from monitoring near Leova. No casualties were reported.

President Maia Sandu said Moscow "cares neither about neutrality, nor sovereignty, nor human life" and that Moldova wants peace but lacks the defence capabilities to stop drones. On 23 October Moldova expelled a member of the Russian embassy after an earlier drone fell near homes.

stories.title: Sudan's army says it took more ground in West Kordofan on 16 November as it advances on the RSF-held city of Al Nahud.
stories.summary: The army said it seized five localities near Abu Zabad on 16 November (Middle East Monitor), and a Sudans Post map dated 17 November puts its front about 60 km east of Al Nahud. Sudan Tribune reports army drone strikes and thousands of civilians fleeing toward Darfur.
stories.heat: Sudan Tribune, Middle East Monitor, Anadolu (via Yeni Safak), Sudans Post, TRT World · velocity: medium, a steady advance over five days, no fighting reported inside the city
detail: New since the last edition, which carried the Abu Qalb drone strike: the army said on Monday 16 November that it took Al-Saatat and other localities northeast of Abu Zabad (Middle East Monitor). Military sources told Anadolu the army earlier took Al-Khuway and then Khamasat, Markab and Umm Oweisha east of Al Nahud. A territorial map by Sudans Post dated 17 November places the army front about 60 km east of the city, which the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) still hold. These are the army's own claims.

Sudan Tribune reports intensive army drone strikes on RSF positions across West Kordofan from 15 November and residents fleeing west from Al Nahud, Abu Zabad and Wad Banda toward Darfur. A local relief committee said RSF fighters killed 10 civilians in Al Nahud and reported looting and a communications blackout (TRT World); that claim has no independent confirmation.
stories.about: Al Nahud is a trading city in West Kordofan on the main road between central Sudan and Darfur. The RSF is the paramilitary force at war with Sudan's army since April 2023.

stories.title: Two explosive drones hit bases of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in Sulaymaniyah, Iraq, on 17 November, two security sources told Reuters.
stories.summary: Reuters gave no casualty or damage figures and no one claimed the attack (via Iran International and Middle East Eye). Iran has struck such bases repeatedly, most recently on 4 November.
stories.heat: Reuters, carried by Iran International, Middle East Eye, This is Beirut · velocity: low to medium, a repeat of the 4 November attack
detail: New, 17 November: two drones carrying explosives attacked bases of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in Sulaymaniyah, in Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, according to two security sources quoted by Reuters. The reports give no casualties and no official Iranian or Iraqi response. Iran accuses these groups of attacks inside Iran and has hit their bases before; Reuters reported a similar strike in Sulaymaniyah and east of Erbil on 4 November. The attribution to Iran is not confirmed for this attack.

stories.title: The RSF released 91 detainees from Shala Prison in El Fasher after about six months, former detainees told Darfur24.
stories.summary: Darfur24 reported on 17 November that the men had been held on suspicion of travelling to army-controlled areas. Released men described overcrowding, food shortages and deaths from untreated illness; the outlet did not independently confirm their accounts.
stories.heat: Darfur24 only · velocity: low, single local report
detail: New, reported 17 November: the Rapid Support Forces freed 91 people from Shala Prison in El Fasher, North Darfur. One released man told Darfur24 that RSF fighters arrested him and eight others near Um Badr in North Kordofan on their way to gold mines in Northern State, held them for days in large containers east of El Fasher, and jailed them without any investigation. He said some detainees were minors and most had no link to the fighting.

A second man described food shortages, poor medical care, skin disease and deaths from chronic illness, and said 21 detainees were moved to Daqris Prison in Nyala. The RSF took El Fasher in October 2025 after a long siege. The report rests on former detainees' accounts to one outlet.

sections.title: India
sections.blurb: Dhoni retires from the IPL, India beat Pakistan for a 10th SAFF title, the Earthshot Prize is awarded in Mumbai, Cyclone Akvan heads for Andhra Pradesh, and Bilkis Bano says she will challenge a bail order.
